text:
===== FILE 15641__1.pdf =====
August 28, 2025  
 
Douglas A. Collins  
Secretary of Veterans Affairs  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs  
810 Vermont Ave., NW 
Washington, DC 20420  
 
Dr. Steven L. Lieberman 
Acting Under Secretary for Health  
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs  
810 Vermont Ave., NW  
Washington, DC 20420  
Submitted Electronically  
RE: 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AS31), Proposed Rule, Reproductive Health Services  
Dear Secretary Collins and Under Secretary Lieberman: 
The National Network of Abortion Funds (NNAF), a national membership organization of 
nearly 100 independent abortion funds, strongly opposes the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ 
(VA) proposed rule to enact one of the most restrictive abortion bans in the nation and to silence 
VA providers from providing information to their patients about abortion. This compounded 
cruelty means that veterans or their family members who are pregnant due to rape or incest, or in 
some cases whose lives or health are in danger, cannot get the essential health care they need from 
the VA and cannot talk to their provider about where or how else to obtain it. Abortion funds exist 
because it is challenging, if not impossible, for many people to overcome misinformation and legal, 
logistical, and structural barriers to get the abortions they want and need. This proposed rule 
exacerbates that bleak reality for veterans and their families, and will likely mean people in crisis 
will be forced to remain pregnant against their will. That is a profound abdication of responsibility 
for an agency directed to “promote, preserve, or restore the health” of our nation’s veterans and 
their families. We urge you to rescind this proposed rule and, at a bare minimum, leave in place 
the current rule enabling VA providers to provide limited abortions and to talk with their patients 
about their full spectrum of health care options. 

 
2 
A. The proposed rule would be one of the most extreme abortion bans in the United 
States.  
In September 2022, following the Supreme Court’s devastating decision in Dobbs v. 
Jackson Women’s Health Organization and in recognition of the increasingly restrictive legal and 
political landscape that followed, the VA expanded abortion access for veterans and their families. 
Before that, the VA had banned abortion care and counseling without exception. With this 
expansion, veterans and eligible family members and caretakers can now access abortions through 
the VA in cases of rape, incest, or when their life or health is in danger. The VA estimates it has 
provided abortions to 140 veterans and their eligible family members each year since Dobbs and 
has covered those abortions as a necessary medical service. All people should be able to get the 
abortions they want and need regardless of the reason and the VA’s coverage of abortion since 
Dobbs should be considered the absolute bare minimum to meet its obligations to veterans and 
their families given the ongoing abortion access crisis.  
Now, the VA proposes to ban nearly all abortions. In effect, this proposed rule means that 
the VA is knowingly and intentionally abandoning veterans and their families. The only exception 
is if a provider “certifies that the life of the” pregnant person “would be endangered” if they do 
not get an abortion. Like all vague and narrow exceptions to abortion bans, this exception will be 
unworkable in all but the most extreme circumstances. It will force VA providers to gamble with 
people’s lives, weighing whether a patient is close enough to death for the exception to apply. This 
would cause chaos, confusion, and delay, as we have seen with other abortion bans across the 
country, and people will die. Of the 18 states with abortion bans or early gestational limits, all but 
4 have at least one exception for rape, incest, or to save the health of the pregnant person. This 
proposed rule has none of those exceptions and would force the pregnant person to remain pregnant 
in all of those situations. If finalized, this rule would be one of the most extreme abortion bans in 
the United States.  
By proposing this rule, the VA casts aside its fundamental obligation to “promote, preserve, 
or restore the health” of veterans and their families. Abortion is a necessary medical service that 
is essential to the health and well-being of veterans and their families, regardless of why someone 
wants or needs an abortion. Whether the VA agrees with that statement or not, it should be 
noncontroversial that providing an abortion to someone who has been raped, assaulted by a family 
member, or whose health is in danger, is consistent with, and necessary to fulfill, that obligation. 
The fact that the VA attempts to frame abortions in these circumstances as “elective” is an 
especially cruel sleight of hand, particularly when we are discussing individuals who have been 
sexually assaulted or are experiencing a medical crisis. That was true when the VA banned abortion 
before, and that cruelty is compounded now that abortion has lost its constitutional protection and 
abortion is illegal or impossible to access for many people throughout the United States. For many 
veterans, the VA is the only place to obtain an abortion where they live: nearly half of veterans of 
reproductive age live in states with abortion bans, and women are the fastest-growing group of 
veterans. If this rule is finalized, they will have nowhere else to go.   

 
3 
That means many veterans will be forced to travel to another state to get an abortion (if 
they have the information, resources, and support to do that) or to remain pregnant against their 
will. Most people cannot afford the cost of an abortion, much less the increased costs to travel 
away from their homes, lives, and communities to get an abortion in another state. Abortion funds 
exist because of that heartbreaking truth. In 2024, abortion funds across the country disbursed 
more than $50 million to pay for abortions for people who could not afford them. And of this $50 
million, over $13 million was specifically for logistical support to make those abortions possible, 
like lodging, transportation, and childcare costs. But as abortion becomes increasingly restricted 
and criminalized, the growing need far outpaces the resources and capacity of abortion funds, and 
across the country, funds are straining under the weight of this demand while the unmet need only 
grows. In 2024, thousands of people were not able to get the financial resources they needed to 
travel for their abortions, jeopardizing their lives, health, and well-being as well as their economic 
security and ability to care for themselves and their families.  
Veterans who cannot find the information, resources, or support to get an abortion 
elsewhere will be forced to remain pregnant. It should go without saying, but given the VA’s 
current position, we will say it anyway: it is a cruel violation of human rights and dignity to 
force another person to stay pregnant against their will. Decades of research have shown that 
being denied a wanted abortion means someone is more likely to experience pregnancy 
complications, more likely to remain in violent personal relationships, and more likely to 
experience poverty and struggle to pay for basic living expenses like food, housing, and 
transportation. Denying abortions to veterans and their families will also exacerbate the entrenched 
and widespread health disparities that already exist in our country. Veterans face unique health 
care challenges, including recovery from combat or service-related trauma, mental health issues, 
and military sexual assault. Denying access to abortions will only exacerbate these health issues 
and others, causing immense harm that will fall most heavily on Black, Indigenous, veterans of 
color, LGBTQI+ veterans, and veterans with disabilities who are more likely to live in places with 
fewer providers, are more likely to struggle to afford the cost of care because of ongoing economic 
inequality, and who already face immense discrimination getting the care they need inside and 
outside of the VA. 
B. The proposed rule compounds the cruelty of this extreme abortion ban by 
prohibiting VA providers from talking to their patients about abortion at all.  
The proposed rule not only bans nearly all abortions, but also prohibits VA providers from 
talking to their patients about abortion at all. By silencing providers from sharing information with 
patients about their other options, the VA makes it clear that the true purpose of this proposed rule 
is to force veterans and their families to remain pregnant against their will, regardless of the 
circumstances or the risks to their lives or health. Patients understandably expect their provider to 
use evidence-based practices to share information about their health and health care options. If 
they cannot get an abortion at the VA and cannot talk about it with their provider, many veterans 
and their family members will have nowhere else to turn. Misinformation about abortion is 

 
4 
rampant, and many people struggle to access accurate and complete information about their 
options when their provider refuses or is unable to tell them how and where they can get 
information and resources. This gag undermines doctors and sends the message that the VA does 
not trust them to provide high quality health care that is in the best interest of their patients.  
This gag also illuminates the cruelty and empty promise of the limited exception if a 
provider “certifies that the life of the” pregnant person “would be endangered” if they do not get 
an abortion. Doctors will be forced to make life-or-death decisions under the weight and fear of 
legal scrutiny. Not only will this inevitably lead to the delay of life- and health-saving care as the 
provider weighs whether the pregnant person is close enough to death to warrant saving, but the 
pregnant person will be cut off from any information or context about their condition, 
circumstances, or options that may enable them to make their own decisions. At the impulse of 
their provider and stuck within a legal framework that denies their humanity or autonomy, pregnant 
people will die. It is hard to ignore the implication that that is precisely the point.  
C. The VA cannot downplay the cruelty of this arbitrary and capricious rule by 
sidestepping its obligations under the Administrative Procedure Act.  
The VA attempts to disguise its motives by reframing this proposed rule as a simple 
“reinstatement” and avoiding the reasoned analysis the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) 
requires. This proposed rule is much more than a “reinstatement” of a prior policy position, and 
the VA knows it. Pre-Dobbs, the VA’s abortion ban meant that veterans and their families could 
not get care at the VA, but abortion was legal and constitutionally protected in all fifty states. Post-
Dobbs, the VA adopted the current rule in recognition of its fundamental obligation to “promote, 
preserve, or restore the health” of veterans and their families within a legal and political landscape 
that had undergone a seismic shift. Now, without constitutional protection and with abortion 
banned or severely restricted in 20 states, the VA knows that finalizing this proposed rule would 
not only mean that veterans and their families would be unable to get abortions at the VA, but that 
they would very likely not be able to get abortions at all. That is a sweeping policy shift that the 
VA must contend with in a thorough and reasoned analysis to meet the requirements of the APA. 
The VA’s misleading, disingenuous, and barebones analysis falls far short of that standard, and 
snubs the community it was created to serve by failing even to mention - much less analyze - the 
immense harm to (or the reliance interests of) hundreds of veterans and their family members. It 
is clear that this policy shift is motivated by anti-abortion animus and cannot withstand the fairness, 
transparency, or accountability the APA requires.  
 
The sweeping cruelty and certain harm this proposed rule will cause should be enough to 
rescind it. But if the VA needs more reason to do so, the proposed rule must also be rescinded 
because it is arbitrary and capricious and violates the VA’s obligations under the APA. If the VA 
has questions about this comment or would like more information about the impact of the proposed 
rule on NNAF’s member funds, please contact MiQuel Davies, Associate General Counsel at 
legal@abortionfunds.org.  

 
5 
Sincerely,  
 
Poonam Dreyfus-Pai 
Interim Executive Director  
National Network of Abortion Funds
